brief_context: Country visited by Ann McMullan.
brief_extract:
AROUND AMERICA IN 30 DAYS
Courtesy: Delta airlines
Ann McMullan, EAW's energetic National Director, spent the whole of September 1980 carrying out an action-packed visit to the USA largely funded and supported by generous and hospitable American organisations and individuals. She covered more than 16,500 miles 'as the crow flies' - but insists, characteristically, that she found the journey more richly rewarding than any mileage-mad crow could ever have done.

location_standardised: Gatwick, West Sussex, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Departure point for flight to Atlanta.
brief_extract: Thanks to the superb efficiency of travel services — especially airlines — in the USA, together with the willing co-operation, kindness and generosity of friendly institutions and organisations, I was able successfully to fulfil these objectives with a minimum of strain, despite enjoying only five completely work-free days out of thirty, instead of the holiday I had planned. I left Gatwick at 12 noon by Delta, that fine American airline, on Monday 1st September, arriving shortly after 4 pm, local time, in Atlanta, Georgia. After a cool, cloudy start in London, it was quite challenging to face 90°F in Atlanta, and what seemed like a mile-long route march to collect my baggage.

Sue Houlding was invited by the Meat Promotion Executive to visit Smithfield Market and talk to the experts about

Buying Beef in Bulk

brief_extract:
Smithfield is Britain's largest meat market and attracts a widespread patronage of buyers from surrounding areas who may even have other markets close to them. The meat from Smithfield is mainly sold to the retail trade in the London area, supplying the eight million or so inhabitants, as well as hotels, the tinned food industries, soap manufacturers, dog food manufacturers, and many other industries. History

The earliest mention of the market dates back to 1174 when Fitstephen, clerk to Thomas à Beckett, described the market as 'A smoothfield where every Friday there is a celebrated rendezvous of fine horses to be sold, and in another quarter are placed vendibles of the peasant, swine with their deep flanks and cows and oxen of immense bulk'.

brief_context: Region from which some meat is imported to the market.
brief_extract: The meat, once sold, is removed from the market shop and taken to the buyers' vans by the porters, each using a large barrow; of the 250 porters employed at Smithfield approximately 100 are self employed and are known as 'bummaree'. It was interesting to note that the greater pecentage of the 3,500 to 4,000 tons of meat which passes through Smithfield is British, although a small percentage comes from the Commonwealth and other countries. brief_context: Mentioned as a place where utility rooms are very popular
brief_extract: One result of the high cost of housing has been that more and more people are tending to stay put and to extend their home in any and every way possible — up into the attic and out over the garage for extra bedrooms; sideways for an additional living room; out from the kitchen for a utility room. The utility room is very popular in Australia and in America, although perhaps not so popular here as it was some 10-15 years ago. However, particularly where the kitchen is small, it can prove an invaluable asset, making it possible to remove from the kitchen such large appliances as the washing machine, tumble dryer and freezer, and also to accommodate all the family clutter such as wellington boots and outdoor coats.

Electricity has become such an integral part of life that consumers expect it to be ‘on-tap’ — just like water: the mere fact that electric power is taken for granted is the highest compliment that can be paid to the efficiency of the supply industry. Sally Fenner visited the CEGB National Control Centre and talked to John Bird, Head of Systems Operation, to find out about the men who make sure that we always have an electricity supply — whatever the time, the place or the demand.
